summary: Specifies the packet format and procedures for running TCP and UDP over IPX networks, so that ordinary TCP/IP applications can work on networks that carry IPX. It is an experimental protocol, not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Different networks speak different languages. This memo explains how to put an Internet message inside an envelope that an IPX network knows how to deliver.

subtitle: Running TCP and UDP protocols on IPX networks so TCP/IP applications work on Novell networks.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP applications cannot run directly on IPX networks (used by Novell NetWare), so administrators must maintain both IPX and IP infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: TCP and UDP are adapted to run over IPX by mapping socket numbers to IPX socket numbers (0x9091 for TCP, 0x9092 for UDP) and replacing IP addresses with IPX addresses in checksums and pseudo-headers. UDP uses a new IPXF fragmentation layer because IPX has no fragmentation support.
tldr.outcome: TCP/IP applications like NFS and HTTP can run directly on IPX networks without requiring IP infrastructure, simplifying network administration in IPX-only shops.

today: RFC 1791 is an Experimental protocol that did not become a standard. While Novell NetWare was widely deployed in the 1990s, the TCP/IP stack eventually became dominant, and most modern networks use IP exclusively. IPX has largely disappeared from production networks, making this specification primarily of historical interest.

sections.title: Motivation and Overview
sections.content:
Novell NetWare and many corporate networks use IPX (Internetwork Packet eXchange) as their network protocol. However, most modern applications are written for TCP/IP and expect to run on the Internet or TCP/IP networks. Administrators running IPX networks who want to use TCP/IP applications (such as HTTP for the Web, NFS for file sharing, or DLsw for bridging legacy protocols) are forced to run IP in addition to IPX, doubling their network management burden.

RFC 1791 solves this by adapting TCP and UDP to run directly over IPX, allowing existing TCP/IP applications to work on IPX networks without modification. The specification defines packet formats, address mappings, and procedures for running both protocols over IPX, enabling applications like HTTP and NFS to function in IPX-only environments.
sections.eli5: Some networks use IPX instead of the standard TCP/IP. This RFC explains how to make TCP and UDP work on IPX networks so that internet programs can run on company networks that use IPX.

sections.title: Socket Numbers and Packet Format
sections.content:
TCP and UDP rely on port numbers to identify which applications are sending and receiving. On IPX, the equivalent is a socket number. RFC 1791 reserves two specific socket numbers:

UDP over IPX uses socket 0x9092. Both source and destination sockets must be this value for UDP packets. Any UDP datagram received with a different source socket is silently discarded. The packet format mirrors standard IPX packets: the IPX header (containing checksums, addresses, and socket numbers) precedes the UDP header and data. Both TCP/IPX and UDP/IPX use IPX packet type 4.

TCP over IPX uses socket 0x9091. Like UDP, both source and destination sockets must be this value. The TCP header and data follow the IPX header in the same packet.

This allocation of reserved socket numbers ensures that TCP and UDP packets destined for these sockets are routed to the correct protocol stack, similar to how IP uses protocol numbers to distinguish TCP (6) from UDP (17).
sections.eli5: TCP and UDP need to know which program to send data to. On IPX networks, each protocol gets a special number: TCP uses 0x9091, UDP uses 0x9092. Every TCP/IPX packet must use its special number as both the source and destination.

sections.title: Checksums and Pseudo-Headers
sections.content:
Both TCP and UDP use checksums to detect corruption. To compute a checksum, they use a pseudo-header containing address and protocol information.

TCP/IP pseudo-headers include source and destination IP addresses and the IP protocol number. The TCP/IPX pseudo-header substitutes IPX source and destination addresses (each comprising a 4-octet network, 6-octet node, and 2-octet socket number) for the IP addresses, and includes the IPX socket numbers instead of a protocol identifier. The remaining fields (zero octet and TCP length) are identical to TCP/IP.

UDP/IPX uses an analogous pseudo-header with IPX addresses and socket numbers replacing IP addresses and the protocol number. The checksum computation itself—a 16-bit one's complement of one's complement sum of all 16-bit words—is unchanged.

If the UDP/IPX checksum computes to zero, it is transmitted as all ones (0xFFFF), and a received checksum of all zeros indicates the sender did not compute a checksum. This matches UDP/IP behavior.
sections.eli5: Checksums are math checks to make sure data didn't get corrupted in transit. To compute them, TCP and UDP need to know the source and destination addresses and protocol type. For IPX, the addresses and socket numbers are substituted into the same formula, and the result is the same.

sections.title: UDP Fragmentation with IPXF
sections.content:
UDP datagrams can be up to 64,000 octets long, but IPX packets are limited by the path's maximum transmission unit (MTU), typically 576 octets or larger. IP has built-in fragmentation support, but IPX does not. To solve this, RFC 1791 introduces the IPXF layer (IPX Fragmentation), which sits between UDP and IPX.

IPXF accepts datagrams up to 64K from UDP and fragments them as needed, prepending an IPXF header to each fragment. Fragments are sent to IPX socket 0x9093 (the IPXF socket). If a datagram fits within the path MTU, IPXF acts as a null layer and forwards it directly to the actual destination socket (0x9092) without a fragmentation header.

The IPXF header preserves the original destination socket number and includes a fragment offset (measured in octets, not 8-octet units like IP), a fragment identification for reassembly, and the original datagram length. The receiving IPXF reassembles fragments back into the complete datagram, restores the original socket number, and delivers it to UDP.

If the path MTU is unknown, IPXF assumes a minimum of 576 octets, meaning datagrams larger than 546 octets (576 minus the IPX header) will be fragmented. TCP does not use IPXF and must instead limit segment size to the path MTU.
sections.eli5: UDP messages can be longer than IPX packets. A new layer called IPXF sits between UDP and IPX and breaks big messages into smaller pieces. At the other end, IPXF puts the pieces back together before handing them to UDP. If the message is already small, IPXF just passes it through unchanged.

sections.title: TCP Segment Size and Multiplexing
sections.content:
Unlike UDP, TCP runs directly over IPX without fragmentation. TCP must therefore limit segment size to avoid exceeding the path MTU. The RFC recommends that implementations either dynamically discover the path MTU for each connection or allow static configuration of a reasonable segment size.

For example, an ethernet-only network might configure TCP segments to 1,470 octets (including the TCP header). If configuration is impossible, the implementation should assume a path MTU of 576 octets and not send TCP segments larger than 546 octets (576 minus the IPX header). Implementers should communicate the chosen maximum segment size to the peer TCP via the MSS (Maximum Segment Size) option in the TCP SYN handshake.

When TCP or UDP runs over both IPX and IP simultaneously, delivery must consider the network layer. The connection endpoint becomes a triplet of (network layer, address, port). First, the implementation attempts to deliver data to the most specific endpoint bound to the network layer the packet arrived on. If no such endpoint exists, it falls back to an endpoint not bound to any specific network layer. This allows a listening socket bound to AF_UNSPEC to accept connections from either IPX or IP networks, while a socket bound to AF_IPX accepts only IPX traffic.
sections.eli5: TCP needs to know how big its packets can be. If you don't tell it, it assumes the smallest safe size (546 octets of data). The two sides agree on the size using an option in the TCP handshake. If a computer is running both IPX and IP, it needs to know which network each connection is on.
